Princeton Electric Speedboating’s “Tiger”
Princeton University
Autonomous Division
The Team:
Autonomous System:
• Calvin Nyugen
• Yash Iyer
Mechanical Design
• Rihan Sajid
• Sean Lee
• Aidan Astudillo
• Andrew Robbins
• Stephen Burns
• Evan Callas
• Andrei Bazavan
Electrical Design
● Norah Smith
● Antoun Salib
● Reiko Zhang
● Andre Graves
● Han Lee
● Tom Wang
● Brandon Wilk
● Nigel Hu
● Luke Hathaway
● Max MachadoBackground & Planing Hull

For the 2025 Promoting Electric Propulsion Manned Planning division PES has chosen to
bring Tiger. Tiger is a 12’ long D Stock hydroplane built in the early 2000’s. PES chose this hull
for a variety of reasons, including but not limited to its efficiency, rough water handling,
flexibility in powertrain, and familiarity.
Firstly the hull is incredibly efficient. In traditional race trim with a gas outboard the
boat's specs are: 50 hp, 550 lbs (with driver), and a top speed of ~80 mph. These values give a
Couch’s constant of 265 which is far higher than all other comparably sized hulls we looked at.
For example the Couch’s constant of a comparable outboard runabout is just 216 and a flat
bottom Jon boat is as low as 136. The Couch’s constant is a non-dimensional term that quantifies
how efficient a hull is based on how fast it goes and the hp it has and its weight. In addition to
being highly efficient in a straight line the hydroplane design is ideal for the 1 mile oval race
course of PEP. The hydroplane is sculpted to turn as hard while maintaining higher corner speeds
unlike a tunnel hull that while it turns tighter will lose more speed in the process.
Secondly PEP historically has not been a totally flat race course. During the 2024 PEP
manned planning event Big Bird (PES’s previous entry) was airborne multiple times at speeds
exceeding 65 mph. This was at a race weight of 990 lbs! In contrast the completed boat with the
driver is <500 lbs this year. Thus we needed a hull that would allow us to go fast with limited
power while maintaining control at high speeds. This D Stock hydroplane offers a nice balance
with it having significantly better rough water handling as compared to its smaller C and B stock
brothers while not being significantly heavier than those crafts.
Furthermore the outboard hydroplane platform offers tremendous opportunities for
powertrain development as the design is simply restricted to an outboard based motor. Thus we
can get wild with our outboard and battery pack (inside the hull) design and have it easily bolt up
to the transom without worry of making motor mounts or propshaft alignment.
Lastly PES is very familiar with the hydroplane hull. Over the last 5 years we have
improved our knowledge of the hull type and how to maximize it’s performance in multiple
modes of operation. Each year making small improvements that compound into significant
increases in speed.
While the hull is a great platform to start from, it needed to be modified to fit our needs.
First the transom height was far too low for our outboard design and we have increased the
height of the transom by adding to the existing transom with a plywood and fiberglass composite
to keep it light and strong. Additionally we painted the bottom of the boat with SpeedCoat49
which is a coating often used by racing teams to reduce drag. It is especially helpful in the
corners when the boat sets down and has a significantly larger wetted area than when aired out
on the straights.Lastly we significantly improved the turnfin on the left side of the hull. Originally it was

perfectly vertically mounted. To improve it we made a billet aluminum mount that canted the fin
at 5 degrees inward. This helps to keep the inner side of the hull close to the water during the
turns, allowing for higher cornering forces without concern of the boat becoming unstable.
Additionally we machined a new turnfin from 7075 aluminum which allowed us to make an even
stiffer fin that is slightly thinner than the original piece and reduces drag.
Propeller
The motor choice was driven by the range of available propellers and the propellers are
then derived from the final motor selection. For 2025 the electric motor makes peak power at
~10,500 rpm, thus under ideal conditions the motor would spend the majority of its time on the
race course near this rpm. This is pretty high for a marine propeller of our size. Thus we have a
1.54:1 reduction in the lower unit to bring the propeller speed down to ~6,800 rpm. While still
quite fast this is within the range of typical outboard racing craft. Our target average speed for
the race course is 50 mph and when assuming 15% slip this gives a propeller pitch of slightly
under 10” of pitch. This fits well with the propellers for the 125cc PRO Outboard Hydroplane
and Runabout classes. They typically run a 10-10.5” pitch propeller. Thus we have 4 125cc PRO
props for testing and race days. These vary in diameter from 6.5-7”. Allowing us to change the
propeller to accommodate the water conditions present on the course that day.Mechanical Systems

The Princeton Electric Speed Boating Mechanical team has made several improvements
from last year. Last year, the design had many components that led to possible misalignment and
vibrations due to poor tolerancing and the use of bolts to create unnecessary connections. This
was somewhat driven by the fact that we machined our old outboard entirely in house. However,
this year we went with a combination of in-house manufacturing and outsourcing. This allowed
us to keep tighter tolerances and have complex parts in our design with alignment features to
guide the assembly. This year, we also went in a new direction with our design philosophy. Last
year, we made an outboard that optimized the aerodynamics of the boat by making the outboard
stationary in areas where it was exposed to air. Our new outboard has a greater focus on a
compact, space-efficient, and portable outboard.
We have chosen to use two coupled outrunner motors which have shaped the direction of
the outboard’s design. This setup prevents the motors from being mounted by its outer body, so a
more complex design is required. Figure _ shows an assembly that holds the bottom motor while
allowing its body to freely rotate. The motors are visibly housed inside of a clear polycarbonate
tube which not only adds a unique aesthetic twist to the outboard, but also allows us to quickly
spot any water leaks that may compromise the motors.
Figure _: Outboard assemblyFigure _: example of FEA on a part receiving thrust load

The cooling system includes a plate heat exchanger and pump. Cold raw water runs from
the lower unit to the heat exchanger to cool a closed-loop flow running through the inverters,
battery pack, and motors.
The motor cowling is designed to provide a waterproof, aerodynamic cover for the
interior components of the outboard. It was fabricated using a fiberglass wet layup. A mold was
constructed from several 3D-printed components with bolted connections. It was then prepped
by applying body filler and primer before wet sanding. Then mold release was applied and the
fiberglass laid up on top. Once finished, a 3D printed interface rim was adhered to the cowl to
latch it down to the outboard with an O-ring sealing mechanism. The cowling also features a port
for all cabling between the battery pack in the boat. The cowling is easily removable to access
the interior system. This presented a risk as any easy release latching mechanism was potentially
less secure, or provided less compressive force than a bolted connection and could result in poor
waterproofing or even part failure.
Many parts that make up the outboard motor have been designed and outsourced to a
machining company called RapidDirect located in Shenzhen, China. As a result, we’ve learned
how to create engineering drawings and tolerance dimensions for proper assembly. We have also
further developed our ability to use machine shop resources.
There are several risks involved with the design. First, the assembly is more complex due
to using two coupled outrunners. This adds complexity with motor alignment and billet
aluminum parts. Second, it was the team’s first time ordering parts from RapidDirect, so there
was risk of receiving incorrectly machined parts. Third, the choice to house the motors inside a
clear tube increases risk of water leakage through edges. This will be thoroughly tested to ensure
confident sealing for competition day, however there are unexpected mishaps that may occur. Electrical Systems

Low Voltage System
The low voltage system for Tiger is built to facilitate the running of small electrical
components on board the boat. It comprises one Dakota Lithium 12V 20AH USB deep cycle
LIFEPO4 battery which acts as a switch for the high voltage contactors, and powers all cooling
and RC circuits. We chose this battery because it has the requisite voltage and current for all of
our low power applications (inverter, RC components, coolant pumps) without excessive heating
or servicing. Moreover, it is lightweight and compact, allowing us to fit it in the watertight high
voltage battery pack. Power distribution is controlled by three switches on the dashboard,
labelled LV, HV, Cooling. The LV switch manages system power for the inverters, and must be
closed for any startup to occur. The HV switch begins precharge and allows for ignition and
power flow from the batteries to the motor, and the Cooling switch allows power to flow from
the LV battery to the coolant pumps. Built into the low voltage system is a remote kill switch
which allows us to safely operate the boat remote control. The switch is a dstfuy long distance
remote DC switch rated for a maximum of 30 amps
High Voltage System
Because of the changes in PEP requirements for the 2024-2025 season, our high voltage
system must be able to run larger amounts of current than we had previously dealt with in order
to provide sufficient power to our motors to reach the speeds we want. This changed our design
for the high voltage system. The HV system is designed to operate at 55V, 400A continuous, and
distributes power from the batteries to two inverters and motors. We were very conscious of the
risks of running high current through this system, and chose high capacity contactors and wires
with very high current carrying capacity to allow the system to operate safely. We are using the
Rincon REC35P1MX Contactor which is rated for 32-95V, 500A continuous, and two 3Schul
Motors C1000 Inverters, which are rated for 36-126V, 500A DC, 1000A Phase. This ensures that
we can run sufficient current through the system for our power needs, but that the contactor trips
long before we damage our electronics with high current. The inverters run on the VESC
software, allowing us to use a suite of established tools to monitor our battery and motor
performance in real time through an app. A phone holder is built into the dashboard so that we
can receive constant speed, temperature, and battery level information in the cockpit. Moreover,
the use of VESC software has allowed us to draw inspiration from similar high voltage projects,
such as electric skateboards and motorcycles through online forums. This has helped us design
our high voltage system while learning from the experiences of other users.
Our speed is controlled by a Single Channel EV West Billet Aluminum Throttle
Potentiometer, which sends signals to our inverters when the RC system is not on. The hand
throttle rotates 90 degrees, allowing us to easily control the speed. Potentiometer signals are
compatible with our VESC based inverters, and the signal is sent in parallel to both inverters.Motors

For our motors, we used two LMT7065 motors. We chose the 7065 because they are the
highest power density motors that we could find at 55V. They fit within our RPM range of 6000-
12000 revolutions per minute which works with the gear boxes we have available. As we were
working with these motors, we had to make some adjustments to our mechanical system, since
these motors operate at the upper end of our RPM range, making it challenging to get peak
performance. Another reason we chose these motors is that the power range is also compatible
with our system. Our target is 20-25 kw continuous, and each motor is rated to do 10-15kw
continuous, which we will be able to utilize.
Remote Control
Competition Updates:
The PEP Unmanned Boat Competition has introduced substantial changes for the 2025
season, influencing both mechanical and electrical design. Each team must now complete two 1-
mile laps around two buoys, with the additional requirement of transporting a 30 to 60 lb payload
as well as maintaining a maximum voltage of 55.5 volts.
This paper outlines the lessons learned from our 2024 implementation, the changes made
for 2025, and the integration and software processes that led to a more reliable, performancefocused, and user-friendly unmanned marine system.
2024 Challenges Recap:
During the 2024 competition, our design was centered around the Teensy microcontroller
and a PandaRC VT5805 module to facilitate remote communication. The control flow consisted
of:
● A Teensy microcontroller connected to the PandaRC VT5805, handling RC
communication
● A second Teensy interfacing with voltage regulators as well as a analog to digital
converter, which in turn controlled linear actuators for steering as well as send out a
analog 5v signal for throttle
● A laptop, via USB, linked to another PandaRC VT5805 module for land-based control
Despite being theoretically rated for a 5-mile range, the PandaRC system demonstrated
an effective range of only 0.5 miles. Additionally, the RC module proved physically fragile—
failing under real-world pressure during competition and stalling the boat. The requirement for a
tethered laptop further complicated deployment and usability.Key failure points included:

● Unreliable RC communication and fragile hardware
● Limited signal range
● Cumbersome setup requiring a laptop for operation
● Inability to complete the race due to communication breakdown
2025 System Improvements
Our revised 2025 system focuses on reliability and robust communication. The goal was
to eliminate the need for fragile hardware and replace it with industry-standard, highperformance components. We also prioritized modularity and safety in both hardware and
software.
Hardware Selection & Rationale
Cube Orange Flight Controller
● The Cube Orange is the core of our unmanned system. It supports open-source software
(ArduPilot and Mission Planner) which allow us to write our own programs and scripts.
● The onboard sensors including the accelerometer, gyroscope, GPS, etc, enable advanced
features such as PID tuning, telemetry, and autonomous decision-making.
Key Features:
● Sensors: Accelerometer, Gyroscope, Compass, Barometer
● Input Voltage: 4.1–5.7V at 2.5A
● Power Output: 14W
● Servo Rail Voltage: 3.3V / 5V
● USB Input: 4–5.7V at 250mA
● Operating Temp: -10°C to 55°C
● Cube Herelink Transmission SystemCube Herelink Transmission System

Replacing the fragile PandaRC module, the Cube Herelink system integrates both RC and HD
video transmission in a single device. It features an onboard controller running Mission Planner,
eliminating the need for a laptop.
Advantages:
● Range: 12.5 miles
● Protocol: MAVLink (highly reliable and widely supported)
● Built-in 4950 mAh battery
● HD video feed with low latency
● Easy integration with Cube flight controller
GoPro Hero 12
● Chosen for its availability in our arsenal and HDR video capability. It also allows us to
record tests and runs and stream to our flight controller via micro-HDMi for visual
feedback and diagnostics.
ODrive S1 + M8325 Motor Kit
Our mechanical requirements demanded a torque output of 50 Nm. Unfortunately, the servo
motors we found online were unable to meet this requirement. Therefore we opted to go for a
brushless DC motor such as the M8325 (5 Nm torque) with a 10:1 gear ratio which allowed us to
achieve the required performance. Additionally, It allows us to easily fix position since the motor
is free spinning rather than locked in.
Specifications:
● DC Voltage Range: 16–48V (compliant with competition rules)
● Modulation Depth: 78%
● Operating Motor Current: 20–80A
● Positional Accuracy via encoder feedback
● Supports self-homing for autonomous operation
●
System Integration & Power
Power Architecture
● Flight Controller: Powered via a 5V buck converter● Herelink System: Powered with a 12V buck converter

● Servo Rail (PWM output): Separate 5V supply for stable PWM signaling
● ODrive Motor Controller: Powered directly via a regulated 16V DC source
Signal and Data Interfacing
● SBUS cable between Herelink and Cube Orange for RC signal
● Video feed routed from GoPro to Herelink via Micro-HDMI
● PWM outputs using 3 pin J connectors from Cube to ODrive controller for throttle and
steering
CAD and Waterproof Housing
Custom CAD enclosures were designed and 3D printed to house:
● Main Box: Flight controller, power electronics
● Antenna Box: Herelink video and RC transmitter
Both housings feature gaskets and sealing mechanisms to ensure waterproofing and
durability in marine environments.
Software Development
Using the open-source ArduPilot ecosystem, we developed our own control scripts and
logic suited for our competition environment.
● Safety Protocols:We modified Mission Planner to only allow system arming upon manual
activation. This prevents accidental activation as well as confirmation that the system is
off when working near the boat.● PWM Optimization: PWM signals for throttle and steering were tuned for signal stability

and responsiveness. Signal frequencies and duty cycles (0–100%) were customized for
each motor output.
● ODrive Self-Homing
○ A custom startup routine enables the steering motor to self-home
○ At boot, the ODrive spins the motor until a mechanical switch is triggered. This
defines the “zero” position. Subsequent movement is calculated via encoder
feedback, allowing precise autonomous steering
System Risks
While the current design is a significant improvement over the previous year, there are still key
risks that could impact system performance and mission success:
Power Drain from Steering Motor
● The steering motor, powered at 16V, may draw excessive current under load—especially
during continuous or sharp maneuvering since the increase in torque will induce an
increase in current (back EMF), drawing more power. This can lead to accelerated
battery depletion, risking power loss mid-race as well as potential risk of overheating.
Mitigation
● This was mitigated by the use of an increased low voltage battery size that could handle
all of the possible energy loss from our unmanned system as well as the installation of
fuses that safeguard the current flowing into our unmanned system.
Loss of RC Communication Link
● Although the Cube Herelink system is rated for long-distance communication (up to 12.5
miles), unforeseen interference—such as electromagnetic noise from onboard systems—
could disrupt the RC or video signals. In such an event, the system is designed to enter a
failsafe mode and shut down, which could prematurely terminate the mission.
● High-frequency interference from the onboard inverter or motor controller may affect
nearby PWM and RC signal lines
Mitigation:
● Unlike last year, we moved the entire unmanned system to the front of the boat, leaving
the inverter and battery near the middle and back of the boat. Therefore, the
electromagnetic interference is significantly lowered. Mechanical Forces Impacting Signal Integrity

● At high speeds or during aggressive turns, the boat experiences significant inertial and
vibrational forces. These could affect signal connectors, wiring, or cause temporary
disconnections in poorly secured systems—leading to signal loss or erratic behavior.
Mitigation
● The entire wiring harness of the unmanned is created using twisted pair signal wires as
well as click on connectors, meaning there is no way for any cable to be disconnected.
By identifying and preparing for these potential risks, we aim to ensure both system safety and
mission continuity during the 2025 PEP competition. Custom Battery Pack

Figure: Modular INR-21700-P45B Battery Pack
Design and Analysis
The design of the battery pack is optimized for thermal management and structural
integrity. The pack consists of 405 3.6V lithium-ion cells1arranged in a configuration with 15 in
series and 27 in parallel to achieve a nominal voltage of 54V and motor current draw
requirements. With each cell rated for 45A discharge, the pack is able to comfortably supply
500A for the duration of the competition. This configuration allows for a modular design such
that groupings of 27 cells could be constructed independently and slid into a structural skeleton.
Due to this modularization, structural components could be 3D printed locally to allow for rapid
design iteration, while also enabling ease of maintenance by being able to remove each rack of
cells.
Air cooling was chosen due to its lightweight, cost-effectiveness, and simplicity
compared to liquid cooling. This design incorporates ventilation channels and strategically
organized cell placement, building on thermal airflow research2to optimize cooling efficiency.
To facilitate active cooling, eight fans3 draw air through a closed airflow loop, optimized for
their high static pressure and airflow characteristics during peak load conditions. Originally built
for desktop computer cooling systems, these fans cycle air through a radiator (connected to an
1 Molicel INR-21700-P45B
2 Zhao, G., & Wang, X. (2022). A design optimization study of an air-cooling battery thermal management system
for electric vehicles. Proceedings of the Institution of Mechanical Engineers, Part D: Journal of Automobile
Engineering. https://doi.org/10.1177/09544089221116418
3 Noctua NF-A14 iPPC-3000 PWMexternal water cooling system), between the cells, and finally through a return duct along the

outside of the pack. Thermal simulation models4allowed us to design to the pack such that
temperature differences across the cooling path remained relatively constant to avoid uneven
thermal load on the cells.
To manage the charging and balancing of the 15 individual cell modules, a BMS system5
was used in a Distributed Group configuration. This system allows for individual module
monitoring and balancing using just 1 G1 Control Unit and 1 CAN Group Module, ensuring even
charge distribution while having simplicity. This system connects to temperature sensors
throughout the pack as well as module taps which monitor and adjust the voltage at different
points in the series connection. This BMS is also compatible with the VESC software used in
the motor inverters, enabling an all-in-one control and monitoring system.
Manufacturing Processes
The structure of the battery pack consists primarily of 3D printed ASA components,
which were chosen due to their excellent shock absorption and heat resistance properties. These
components ensure that the batteries remain securely in place during operation. A watertight
cowling, inspired by Danecca battery packs, was implemented to protect the battery from water
ingress. This allows the internal structure and functionality of the pack to be separated from the
enclosure, which serves as a protective housing and directs airflow for cooling.
Electrical connections between cells within the battery were carefully designed to
minimize resistance and prevent overheating due to varied current draw. Running across the top
of each adjacent 27-cell parallel group is a waterjet sheet of nickel plated copper6. This unique
material features low internal resistance (ρ = 2.874 x 10-8 Ωm) to minimize operational losses to
heat while having a high surface resistance to facilitate easy heat generation during the spot
welding process. Additionally, its high flexibility (UTS = 368 MPa) allows the connections to be
robust to use in rough environments, a necessary feature for a pack onboard a boat crashing
through waves. Spot welding was employed to establish high-quality bonds between cells and
custom waterjet buses and terminals. Additionally, positioning pins on printed cell holders were
added to position the busbar plates while spot welding. Dimples were added to busbar plate tabs
to decrease the resistance between parallel tabs when spot welding, allowing for cleaner welds to
go through the battery with lower current.
4 Models used are from About Energy https://www.aboutenergy.io/
5 EMUS G1 BMS
6 SIGMACLAD 60 from Engineered Materials SolutionsFigure: 3x9 Parallel Module & Modular Rack

Risks and Mitigation Strategies
One of the primary risks associated with the battery pack is thermal runaway, a product
of drawing too much current from the cells. To mitigate this, temperature sensors were placed
within the ventilation channels at various points to monitor and report critical temperatures and
cutoff operation past a given threshold. Mechanical failure due to vibrations or in the event of a
crash posed another challenge. Having an independent pack design from the rigid outer enclosure
allows it to act as an exoskeleton protecting the internal components. Having several channels
running along the length of the cell modules provides a robust attachment point to prevent the
battery from moving around.. In case of extreme jostling and deflection, though the components
should not break, adhesive neoprene insulators along the intermodular conductors between
vertical racks to provide short-circuit protection, and enclosed channels for terminal busbars
were used to isolate the battery pack from the aluminum baseplate.

was risk of receiving incorrectly machined parts. Third, the choice to house the motors inside a
clear tube increases risk of water leakage through edges. This will be thoroughly tested to ensure
confident sealing for competition day, however there are unexpected mishaps that may occur. Electrical Systems
Low Voltage System
The low voltage system for Tiger is built to facilitate the running of small electrical
components on board the boat. It comprises one Dakota Lithium 12V 20AH USB deep cycle
LIFEPO4 battery which acts as a switch for the high voltage contactors, and powers all cooling
and RC circuits. We chose this battery because it has the requisite voltage and current for all of
our low power applications (inverter, RC components, coolant pumps) without excessive heating
or servicing. Moreover, it is lightweight and compact, allowing us to fit it in the watertight high
voltage battery pack. Power distribution is controlled by three switches on the dashboard,
labelled LV, HV, Cooling. The LV switch manages system power for the inverters, and must be
closed for any startup to occur. The HV switch begins precharge and allows for ignition and
power flow from the batteries to the motor, and the Cooling switch allows power to flow from
the LV battery to the coolant pumps. Built into the low voltage system is a remote kill switch
which allows us to safely operate the boat remote control. The switch is a dstfuy long distance
remote DC switch rated for a maximum of 30 amps
High Voltage System
Because of the changes in PEP requirements for the 2024-2025 season, our high voltage
system must be able to run larger amounts of current than we had previously dealt with in order
to provide sufficient power to our motors to reach the speeds we want. This changed our design
for the high voltage system. The HV system is designed to operate at 55V, 400A continuous, and
distributes power from the batteries to two inverters and motors. We were very conscious of the
risks of running high current through this system, and chose high capacity contactors and wires
with very high current carrying capacity to allow the system to operate safely. We are using the
Rincon REC35P1MX Contactor which is rated for 32-95V, 500A continuous, and two 3Schul
Motors C1000 Inverters, which are rated for 36-126V, 500A DC, 1000A Phase. This ensures that
we can run sufficient current through the system for our power needs, but that the contactor trips
long before we damage our electronics with high current. The inverters run on the VESC
software, allowing us to use a suite of established tools to monitor our battery and motor
performance in real time through an app. A phone holder is built into the dashboard so that we
can receive constant speed, temperature, and battery level information in the cockpit. Moreover,
the use of VESC software has allowed us to draw inspiration from similar high voltage projects,
such as electric skateboards and motorcycles through online forums. This has helped us design
our high voltage system while learning from the experiences of other users.
Our speed is controlled by a Single Channel EV West Billet Aluminum Throttle
Potentiometer, which sends signals to our inverters when the RC system is not on. The hand
throttle rotates 90 degrees, allowing us to easily control the speed. Potentiometer signals are
compatible with our VESC based inverters, and the signal is sent in parallel to both inverters.Motors
For our motors, we used two LMT7065 motors. We chose the 7065 because they are the
highest power density motors that we could find at 55V. They fit within our RPM range of 6000-
12000 revolutions per minute which works with the gear boxes we have available. As we were
working with these motors, we had to make some adjustments to our mechanical system, since
these motors operate at the upper end of our RPM range, making it challenging to get peak
performance. Another reason we chose these motors is that the power range is also compatible
with our system. Our target is 20-25 kw continuous, and each motor is rated to do 10-15kw
continuous, which we will be able to utilize.
Remote Control
Competition Updates:
The PEP Unmanned Boat Competition has introduced substantial changes for the 2025
season, influencing both mechanical and electrical design. Each team must now complete two 1-
mile laps around two buoys, with the additional requirement of transporting a 30 to 60 lb payload
as well as maintaining a maximum voltage of 55.5 volts.
This paper outlines the lessons learned from our 2024 implementation, the changes made
for 2025, and the integration and software processes that led to a more reliable, performancefocused, and user-friendly unmanned marine system.
2024 Challenges Recap:
During the 2024 competition, our design was centered around the Teensy microcontroller
and a PandaRC VT5805 module to facilitate remote communication. The control flow consisted
of:
● A Teensy microcontroller connected to the PandaRC VT5805, handling RC
communication
● A second Teensy interfacing with voltage regulators as well as a analog to digital
converter, which in turn controlled linear actuators for steering as well as send out a
analog 5v signal for throttle
● A laptop, via USB, linked to another PandaRC VT5805 module for land-based control
Despite being theoretically rated for a 5-mile range, the PandaRC system demonstrated
an effective range of only 0.5 miles. Additionally, the RC module proved physically fragile—
failing under real-world pressure during competition and stalling the boat. The requirement for a
tethered laptop further complicated deployment and usability.Key failure points included:
● Unreliable RC communication and fragile hardware
● Limited signal range
● Cumbersome setup requiring a laptop for operation
● Inability to complete the race due to communication breakdown
2025 System Improvements
Our revised 2025 system focuses on reliability and robust communication. The goal was
to eliminate the need for fragile hardware and replace it with industry-standard, highperformance components. We also prioritized modularity and safety in both hardware and
software.
Hardware Selection & Rationale
Cube Orange Flight Controller
● The Cube Orange is the core of our unmanned system. It supports open-source software
(ArduPilot and Mission Planner) which allow us to write our own programs and scripts.
● The onboard sensors including the accelerometer, gyroscope, GPS, etc, enable advanced
features such as PID tuning, telemetry, and autonomous decision-making.
Key Features:
● Sensors: Accelerometer, Gyroscope, Compass, Barometer
● Input Voltage: 4.1–5.7V at 2.5A
● Power Output: 14W
● Servo Rail Voltage: 3.3V / 5V
● USB Input: 4–5.7V at 250mA
● Operating Temp: -10°C to 55°C
● Cube Herelink Transmission SystemCube Herelink Transmission System
Replacing the fragile PandaRC module, the Cube Herelink system integrates both RC and HD
video transmission in a single device. It features an onboard controller running Mission Planner,
eliminating the need for a laptop.
Advantages:
● Range: 12.5 miles
● Protocol: MAVLink (highly reliable and widely supported)
● Built-in 4950 mAh battery
● HD video feed with low latency
● Easy integration with Cube flight controller
GoPro Hero 12
● Chosen for its availability in our arsenal and HDR video capability. It also allows us to
record tests and runs and stream to our flight controller via micro-HDMi for visual
feedback and diagnostics.
ODrive S1 + M8325 Motor Kit
Our mechanical requirements demanded a torque output of 50 Nm. Unfortunately, the servo
motors we found online were unable to meet this requirement. Therefore we opted to go for a
brushless DC motor such as the M8325 (5 Nm torque) with a 10:1 gear ratio which allowed us to
achieve the required performance. Additionally, It allows us to easily fix position since the motor
is free spinning rather than locked in.
Specifications:
● DC Voltage Range: 16–48V (compliant with competition rules)
● Modulation Depth: 78%
● Operating Motor Current: 20–80A
● Positional Accuracy via encoder feedback
● Supports self-homing for autonomous operation
System Integration & Power
Power Architecture
● Flight Controller: Powered via a 5V buck converter● Herelink System: Powered with a 12V buck converter
● Servo Rail (PWM output): Separate 5V supply for stable PWM signaling
● ODrive Motor Controller: Powered directly via a regulated 16V DC source
Signal and Data Interfacing
● SBUS cable between Herelink and Cube Orange for RC signal
● Video feed routed from GoPro to Herelink via Micro-HDMI
● PWM outputs using 3 pin J connectors from Cube to ODrive controller for throttle and
steering
CAD and Waterproof Housing
Custom CAD enclosures were designed and 3D printed to house:
● Main Box: Flight controller, power electronics
● Antenna Box: Herelink video and RC transmitter
Both housings feature gaskets and sealing mechanisms to ensure waterproofing and
durability in marine environments.
Software Development
Using the open-source ArduPilot ecosystem, we developed our own control scripts and
logic suited for our competition environment.
● Safety Protocols:We modified Mission Planner to only allow system arming upon manual
activation. This prevents accidental activation as well as confirmation that the system is
off when working near the boat.● PWM Optimization: PWM signals for throttle and steering were tuned for signal stability
and responsiveness. Signal frequencies and duty cycles (0–100%) were customized for
each motor output.
● ODrive Self-Homing
○ A custom startup routine enables the steering motor to self-home
○ At boot, the ODrive spins the motor until a mechanical switch is triggered. This
defines the “zero” position. Subsequent movement is calculated via encoder
feedback, allowing precise autonomous steering
System Risks
While the current design is a significant improvement over the previous year, there are still key
risks that could impact system performance and mission success:
Power Drain from Steering Motor
● The steering motor, powered at 16V, may draw excessive current under load—especially
during continuous or sharp maneuvering since the increase in torque will induce an
increase in current (back EMF), drawing more power. This can lead to accelerated
battery depletion, risking power loss mid-race as well as potential risk of overheating.
Mitigation
● This was mitigated by the use of an increased low voltage battery size that could handle
all of the possible energy loss from our unmanned system as well as the installation of
fuses that safeguard the current flowing into our unmanned system.
Loss of RC Communication Link
● Although the Cube Herelink system is rated for long-distance communication (up to 12.5
miles), unforeseen interference—such as electromagnetic noise from onboard systems—
could disrupt the RC or video signals. In such an event, the system is designed to enter a
failsafe mode and shut down, which could prematurely terminate the mission.
● High-frequency interference from the onboard inverter or motor controller may affect
nearby PWM and RC signal lines
Mitigation:
● Unlike last year, we moved the entire unmanned system to the front of the boat, leaving
the inverter and battery near the middle and back of the boat. Therefore, the
electromagnetic interference is significantly lowered. Mechanical Forces Impacting Signal Integrity
● At high speeds or during aggressive turns, the boat experiences significant inertial and
vibrational forces. These could affect signal connectors, wiring, or cause temporary
disconnections in poorly secured systems—leading to signal loss or erratic behavior.
Mitigation
● The entire wiring harness of the unmanned is created using twisted pair signal wires as
well as click on connectors, meaning there is no way for any cable to be disconnected.
By identifying and preparing for these potential risks, we aim to ensure both system safety and
mission continuity during the 2025 PEP competition. Custom Battery Pack
Figure: Modular INR-21700-P45B Battery Pack
Design and Analysis
The design of the battery pack is optimized for thermal management and structural
integrity. The pack consists of 405 3.6V lithium-ion cells1arranged in a configuration with 15 in
series and 27 in parallel to achieve a nominal voltage of 54V and motor current draw
requirements. With each cell rated for 45A discharge, the pack is able to comfortably supply
500A for the duration of the competition. This configuration allows for a modular design such
that groupings of 27 cells could be constructed independently and slid into a structural skeleton.
Due to this modularization, structural components could be 3D printed locally to allow for rapid
design iteration, while also enabling ease of maintenance by being able to remove each rack of
cells.
Air cooling was chosen due to its lightweight, cost-effectiveness, and simplicity
compared to liquid cooling. This design incorporates ventilation channels and strategically
organized cell placement, building on thermal airflow research2to optimize cooling efficiency.
To facilitate active cooling, eight fans3 draw air through a closed airflow loop, optimized for
their high static pressure and airflow characteristics during peak load conditions. Originally built
for desktop computer cooling systems, these fans cycle air through a radiator (connected to an

outside of the pack. Thermal simulation models4allowed us to design to the pack such that
temperature differences across the cooling path remained relatively constant to avoid uneven
thermal load on the cells.
To manage the charging and balancing of the 15 individual cell modules, a BMS system5
was used in a Distributed Group configuration. This system allows for individual module
monitoring and balancing using just 1 G1 Control Unit and 1 CAN Group Module, ensuring even
charge distribution while having simplicity. This system connects to temperature sensors
throughout the pack as well as module taps which monitor and adjust the voltage at different
points in the series connection. This BMS is also compatible with the VESC software used in
the motor inverters, enabling an all-in-one control and monitoring system.
Manufacturing Processes
The structure of the battery pack consists primarily of 3D printed ASA components,
which were chosen due to their excellent shock absorption and heat resistance properties. These
components ensure that the batteries remain securely in place during operation. A watertight
cowling, inspired by Danecca battery packs, was implemented to protect the battery from water
ingress. This allows the internal structure and functionality of the pack to be separated from the
enclosure, which serves as a protective housing and directs airflow for cooling.
Electrical connections between cells within the battery were carefully designed to
minimize resistance and prevent overheating due to varied current draw. Running across the top
of each adjacent 27-cell parallel group is a waterjet sheet of nickel plated copper6. This unique
material features low internal resistance (ρ = 2.874 x 10-8 Ωm) to minimize operational losses to
heat while having a high surface resistance to facilitate easy heat generation during the spot
welding process. Additionally, its high flexibility (UTS = 368 MPa) allows the connections to be
robust to use in rough environments, a necessary feature for a pack onboard a boat crashing
through waves. Spot welding was employed to establish high-quality bonds between cells and
custom waterjet buses and terminals. Additionally, positioning pins on printed cell holders were
added to position the busbar plates while spot welding. Dimples were added to busbar plate tabs
to decrease the resistance between parallel tabs when spot welding, allowing for cleaner welds to
go through the battery with lower current.

Risks and Mitigation Strategies
One of the primary risks associated with the battery pack is thermal runaway, a product
of drawing too much current from the cells. To mitigate this, temperature sensors were placed
within the ventilation channels at various points to monitor and report critical temperatures and
cutoff operation past a given threshold. Mechanical failure due to vibrations or in the event of a
crash posed another challenge. Having an independent pack design from the rigid outer enclosure
allows it to act as an exoskeleton protecting the internal components. Having several channels
running along the length of the cell modules provides a robust attachment point to prevent the
battery from moving around.. In case of extreme jostling and deflection, though the components
should not break, adhesive neoprene insulators along the intermodular conductors between
vertical racks to provide short-circuit protection, and enclosed channels for terminal busbars
were used to isolate the battery pack from the aluminum baseplate.
